video.title: Evaluating agents: Benchmarks, pass@k and variance
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Charts draw themselves; code is typed out on a card, left to right in both languages. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Dr Salma - statistics lecturer, Cairo University (main character)
Prof Farah - head of department, Amman
Narrator - the Darsi voice, talking to a university lecturer (warm, collegial, precise)

scenes.narration: A student team reports that their coding agent solves ninety percent of tasks. When you rerun it, it solves sixty. They ran it once, on tasks they wrote while building it. What should they have done?
Today: how to measure whether an agent works, what pass at k really means, and how to teach students to report results that others can trust.

An evaluation runs an agent on a fixed set of tasks with an automatic check of success. The tasks must be separate from those used to build the agent. And because agents are random, it must be run more than once.

pass at k is the probability that at least one of k attempts succeeds. If one attempt succeeds with probability p, pass at k is one minus one minus p, to the power k. It rewards retries, so report pass at one as well.

On fifty tasks, a sixty percent success rate has a standard error of about seven points. So ninety and sixty may partly be noise and partly overfitting. Report the mean over several runs with an interval.

Public benchmarks may already appear in a model's training data, which inflates scores. Agents can also game a weak checker, for example by editing the tests. Hold out fresh tasks and inspect failures and successes by hand.

In student agent projects, grade the evaluation as seriously as the agent. Require a held-out task set, several runs, pass at one with an interval, and a short error analysis. A modest honest result should earn more than an inflated one.
Quick check! An agent succeeds on a single attempt with probability zero point two. What is pass at two?
Zero point three six: one minus zero point eight squared. Two tries nearly double the headline number, which is why pass at one matters.
In the app, open the Test an agent lab. Run Darsi Tiny on its thirty-two test requests and read every failure. Run it again: the score stays the same, because it always picks the likeliest token.
Your turn. Which result is most trustworthy for a student agent project?
Pass at one averaged over five runs on held-out tasks, with an interval. Remember: separate test tasks, several runs, honest metrics, and read the transcripts.
